articles.title: Old Testament Summary (2): From Moses to Solomon
articles.text: From Moses to Solomon: Family Read-Aloud Guide (Part 2) 📖 Old Testament Part 2 From Moses to Solomon Told for family reading · Inspired by the Greater Catechism, “A Brief History of Religion.” In this journey Egypt: peace that turns into slavery Moses: a child saved for a mission The first Passover The Exodus and the crossing of the Red Sea The wilderness: freedom without obedience is not enough Mount Sinai and the Ten Commandments The Tabernacle and the Ark Complaints and a sign of salvation Joshua and the Promised Land Job: faithfulness in suffering The time of the Judges Saul and David Solomon: wisdom and danger The division of the kingdom The kingdom of Israel and its fall The kingdom of Judah and Babylon What it teaches a family The descendants of Jacob—the Hebrews or Israelites—lived for a time in Egypt in relative peace. At first they were tolerated and respected. But over the years they multiplied until they became a numerous people within that land. 01 Egypt: peace that turns into slavery A new Pharaoh came to power who looked upon the Hebrews not with gratitude or justice, but with fear and harshness. He subjected them to heavy labor and cruel bondage. His oppression reached a terrible extreme: he ordered that every newborn Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile River. That decision sought to cut off the future of the people. It attacked not only the children, but also families, hope, and God's promises. 02 Moses: a child saved for a mission In the midst of that persecution, Moses was born. By a special providence he was saved from the waters of the Nile and taken in by Pharaoh's daughter, who brought him to the royal court, where he received an education and training. God was quietly preparing the man He would use to free His people. When Moses grew up, the Lord commanded him to appear before Pharaoh with his brother Aaron and ask him to let the Hebrews go. But Pharaoh refused: his heart remained hardened, even in the face of God's signs. Then Egypt was struck with ten plagues, severe and extraordinary signs intended to break the king's stubbornness. The last was the death of the Egyptian firstborn, from Pharaoh's own son to the firstborn of the animals. 03 The first Passover: prepared to depart On the night of that final plague, God commanded the Hebrews to celebrate the Passover for the first time. Each family was to sacrifice a spotless lamb, mark the door of the house with its blood, and eat it in haste, ready to set out. The blood on the doors would be a sign of protection: the angel would pass over those houses without striking them. Passover marked the passing of the Lord and the beginning of liberation. That lamb foreshadowed Jesus Christ, the spotless Lamb whose blood saves from eternal death. ✝️ Cf. Jn 1:29 📌 For the family: when God calls us out of slavery, it is not enough to desire freedom. We must obey, prepare ourselves, and walk. 04 The Exodus from Egypt and the crossing of the Red Sea After the death of their firstborn, the Egyptians urged the Hebrews to leave, even giving them gold, silver, and other possessions. The people departed and, after three days, reached the shore of the Red Sea. But Pharaoh regretted letting them go. He gathered his army and pursued them. The Hebrews found themselves trapped between the sea and the troops, and fear overtook them. Moses encouraged the people to trust. He stretched out his staff over the sea, and the waters parted, leaving a dry path across which they walked. Pharaoh, blinded by his stubbornness, also entered with his army; but as they advanced, the waters returned over them, and they were buried in the sea. God had freed Israel from a slavery that had seemed impossible to break. 05 The wilderness: freedom without obedience is not enough After crossing the Red Sea, the Hebrews entered the wilderness. The journey to the Promised Land could have been much shorter, but the people repeatedly rebelled against God and against Moses. Because of their disobedience, God allowed them to remain in the wilderness for forty years. Of those who left Egypt as adults, only Caleb and Joshua entered the Promised Land. Even so, God never stopped caring for them. He gave them manna, a small white food that covered the ground each morning; each day they gathered what they needed, and before the Sabbath they gathered twice as much, because that day was reserved for holy rest. He also brought water from the rock when Moses struck it with his staff. And a cloud protected them from the sun by day, becoming a pillar of fire by night to light the way. 🌿 Today's lesson: God can free a family from many forms of slavery, but that freedom must be lived with obedience, gratitude, and discipline. 06 Mount Sinai and the Ten Commandments Three months after leaving Egypt, the Hebrews arrived at Mount Sinai. There God revealed His presence with mighty signs and gave them His law. The Ten Commandments were written on two stone tablets and given to Moses. They were not merely an external rule: they were the way to order the life of the people before God, within the family, and in society. While Moses remained on the mountain for forty days speaking with the Lord, the people fell into idolatry. They made a golden calf and worshiped it. They had been freed from Egypt, but they still carried within them the disorder of an unfaithful heart. When Moses came down, he saw that grave sin. Filled with zeal for God, he broke the tablets, destroyed the idol, and punished the chief offenders. Then he went back up the mountain, pleaded for the people, and received the tablets again. When he came down, his face shone because he had been in the Lord's presence. 🔥 For the home: faith does not preserve itself. If it is not cared for, the heart creates its own idols: comfort, fear, money, pride, or power. 07 The Tabernacle and the Ark: God among His people At the foot of Mount Sinai, Moses built the Tabernacle according to God's instructions: a great sacred tent set up in the middle of the camp whenever the people stopped. The Ark of the Covenant was also made, a precious chest overlaid with gold. Inside were placed the tablets of the law, a jar of manna, and Aaron's staff that had blossomed. The Tabernacle reminded the people that God was not a distant idea: He accompanied His people on their journey. The Ark was the sign of His covenant, His law, and His protection. In family life, this helps us understand that faith needs a visible center: prayer, reverence for what is holy, remembrance of what has been received, and faithfulness to what God commands. 08 Complaints, punishments, and a sign of salvation During the journey, the Hebrews complained many times against Moses and against God. Their grumbling was not merely weariness; it often expressed distrust, ingratitude, and rebellion. One of the most remembered punishments was that of the venomous serpents. Many were bitten and died. When the people acknowledged their sin, God commanded Moses to raise a bronze serpent on a pole: whoever looked at it with faith was healed. Just as the wounded Israelites looked upon the raised serpent to be healed, the Christian looks to Christ crucified to receive life and healing from sin. ✝️ Cf. Jn 3:14–15 09 Joshua and the entrance into the Promised Land After forty years, the time came to enter the Promised Land. Moses was allowed to see it from afar, but he did not enter. Joshua was chosen to succeed him and lead the people. The Israelites crossed the Jordan River preceded by the Ark: the waters stopped, leaving the riverbed dry. Then they captured Jericho and advanced against the peoples of Canaan. The land was divided among the tribes of Israel, which bore the names of the sons of Jacob and the sons of Joseph: Reuben Simeon Levi Judah Issachar Zebulun Dan Naphtali Gad Asher Benjamin Ephraim Manasseh The tribe of Levi did not receive a territory like the others: it was set apart for priestly service, because God Himself would be its portion and inheritance. And from the tribe of Judah, according to Jacob's prophecy before his death, the Redeemer of the world would later be born. 10 Job: faithfulness in the midst of suffering At that time there lived in Idumea a righteous man named Job. He was wealthy, respected, and God-fearing, striving to turn away from evil. God allowed him to be tested with severe suffering: in a short time he lost his possessions, his children, and his health, and his body became covered with painful sores. In spite of everything, Job did not rebel. Falling to the ground, he worshiped the Lord: The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. 📖 Job 1:21 Job did not understand everything that was happening to him, but he never ceased to acknowledge God as Lord. In the end, God rewarded his patience, restored his health, and granted him greater blessings than before. His story teaches that faith is not genuine only when everything goes well: it is also revealed in loss, illness, and trial. 11 The time of the Judges After conquering Palestine under Joshua's leadership, the Hebrews remained in that land. They were governed by the Law of Moses, by the elders, and, for a long period, by judges: people raised up by God to deliver the nation whenever, because of its sins, it fell under the power of its enemies. Among them were also courageous women, such as Deborah and Jael. Samson He received extraordinary strength and for years fought against the Philistines, Israel's powerful enemies. Later he was betrayed and lost his strength. In the end, gathering what remained of his vigor, he brought down a Philistine temple, dying along with many of his enemies. Samuel He was the last of the judges. After defeating the Philistines, he gathered the people at God's command. The Israelites wanted a king; then Samuel anointed Saul, of the tribe of Benjamin, as the first king of Israel. 12 Saul and David: obedience, downfall, and God's choice Saul reigned for many years. At first he was accepted, but later he was rejected by God because of a serious act of disobedience. Then God chose David, a young man from the tribe of Judah, who became famous by defeating Goliath, a Philistine giant who challenged and insulted God's people. Later, Saul was defeated by the Philistines and took his own life. David ascended the throne and reigned for forty years. He completed the conquest of Palestine, subdued the remaining enemies, and captured Jerusalem, making it the capital of the kingdom. 🕊️ Lesson: authority is not sustained by position alone. It requires obedience to God, humility, and faithfulness. 13 Solomon: wisdom, glory, and spiritual danger David was succeeded by his son Solomon, renowned for his extraordinary wisdom. During his reign, the Temple of Jerusalem was built, the central work of the people's religious life. He enjoyed a long and glorious reign. However, toward the end of his life he allowed himself to be led astray by foreign influences and fell into idolatry. For this reason, some have feared for his eternal salvation. A person may begin well, receive great gifts, and yet still go astray if faithfulness is neglected. Wisdom does not protect when the heart ceases to obey God. ⚠️ Warning from the account 14 The division of the kingdom After Solomon, his son Rehoboam became king. The people asked for relief from the heavy taxes inherited from the previous reign, but Rehoboam refused to listen or lighten those burdens. As a result, ten tribes rebelled and followed Jeroboam, leader of the uprising. Only Judah and Benjamin remained loyal to Rehoboam. Thus the Hebrew people were divided into two kingdoms: the kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah, which were never reunited. 📌 A word for families: when those in authority refuse to listen, place unfair burdens on others, or respond harshly, they can break what they were meant to protect. 15 The kingdom of Israel and its fall The kingdom of Israel had nineteen kings. All of them were wicked and promoted idolatry, leading much of the people away from God. After two hundred fifty-four years, the kingdom was destroyed. As punishment for its grave sins, part of the people was scattered and another part was taken captive to Assyria by Shalmaneser. The kingdom of Israel fell permanently in 722 BC . To repopulate the region, colonies of Gentile peoples were brought in. Over time they mixed with some Israelites who returned from exile and with unfaithful Jews. From this mixture arose the Samaritan people, who eventually developed deep hostility toward the Jews. Among the Israelites taken captive to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, was Tobit, a righteous and God-fearing man. His story teaches us to value holy fear of God and to trust in divine providence even in a foreign land. 16 The kingdom of Judah and the Babylonian captivity The kingdom of Judah had twenty kings. Some were godly and sought to obey the Lord; others committed grave sins. Altogether, they reigned for three hundred eighty-eight years. During the reign of Manasseh, one of the last kings, the story of Judith takes place. She killed Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, and saved Bethulia and Judea from a deadly threat. Later, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, brought the kingdom of Judah to an end. He captured Jerusalem, destroyed the city, and razed Solomon's Temple. He took Zedekiah, the last king, prisoner, put out his eyes, and carried the people away captive to Babylon. Thus ended a painful chapter. The Promised Land, the Temple, and the kingdom were lost because of the accumulated unfaithfulness of the people and their rulers. 17 What this story teaches a family This part of sacred history is not merely a succession of kings, wars, and punishments. It shows how God guides, corrects, sustains, and fulfills His promises. It also teaches that freedom requires obedience: a people may leave Egypt and still remain slaves within if they do not learn to trust God. 🙏 God hears the cry of the oppressed. 🚪 Obedience opens a path even where there seems to be no way. ⚠️ Complaining and idolatry destroy trust. ⚖️ Authority must be exercised with justice and the fear of God. 🏚️ Prosperity without faithfulness can end in ruin. 🌿 Patience in trial, like Job's, is a spiritual strength. 🕯️ Family history is built with memory, responsibility, and faith. A wise family learns from Israel: it remembers what God has done, avoids the idols that disorder the heart, walks together through hardship, and keeps the faith even when the journey passes through the wilderness. ✨ Recommended Products St. Joseph Edition, Catholic Bible View on Amazon Catechism of Saint Pius X View on Amazon 1962 Roman Daily Missal View on Amazon Revelations View on Amazon Hell and Its Torments View on Amazon The place where God dwells View on Amazon As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. articles.title: Old Testament Summary (3): From the Prophets to Christ
articles.text: Old Testament Summary: From Prophets to Christ – Family Guide 📖 Old Testament · Part 3 From the Prophets to Christ Told for family reading, inspired by A Short History of Religion in The Catechism of Saint Pius X. In this journey 1 · Daniel: faithfulness in a foreign land 2 · The end of captivity and return to Judea 3 · Esther: providence among a scattered people 4 · A recovered freedom, yet fragile 5 · Antiochus Epiphanes and the test of faith 6 · The Maccabees: faith and homeland 7 · Judas Maccabeus: courage and prayer 8 · When children lose their parents' virtue 9 · Rome, Herod, and the end of the kingdom 10 · The prophets: remembering the truth 11 · Preparing the people for the Messiah 12 · Prophecies about the time of the Messiah 13 · Fulfillment in Jesus Christ 14 · What it teaches families 1 Daniel: faithfulness in a foreign land During the Babylonian captivity, the prophet Daniel lived there, one of the Hebrew youths chosen to be trained in the royal court and serve the king. Though far from his homeland, Daniel did not abandon the faith of his fathers. His integrity, wisdom, and faithfulness to God earned him the esteem of Nebuchadnezzar, especially when—with divine help—he revealed and interpreted a dream the king had forgotten. Later, he was also esteemed by King Darius. But envious men sought his downfall: they accused him of continuing to pray to his God despite a decree forbidding it. For this faithfulness, he was thrown into the lions' den. God protected him miraculously. Daniel emerged unharmed, showing that obedience to God is worth more than fear of men. 👨‍👩‍👧 For families: faith is not lived only when all is favorable, but also when the environment pressures against it. 2 The end of captivity and return to Judea The exile in Babylon lasted seventy years. Afterward, the Jews obtained from Cyrus permission to return to their land. Led by Zerubbabel, they returned to Judea and began rebuilding Jerusalem and the Temple. It was no easy task: it required perseverance, unity, and spiritual encouragement. Nehemiah, who served the king, and the prophet Haggai encouraged the people to carry forward that holy work. The rebuilding was not merely material. Reconstructing the Temple meant restoring the center of the people's religious life: a concrete way of putting God back at the heart of the nation. 🌿 For families: a home may also need rebuilding. Sometimes it's not walls, but habits, prayer, order, trust, work, and faithfulness. 3 Esther: providence among a scattered people Not all Jews returned to Judea. Many remained in foreign lands. Among them was Esther. By divine providence, Esther became wife of King Ahasuerus. From that position, she was able to save her people when they were threatened with destruction by a royal decree influenced by Haman, the minister who hated Mordecai, Esther's uncle. God can act even when His people seem weak, scattered, or defenseless. A faithful person, placed in the right position, can be an instrument of salvation for many. 4 A recovered freedom, yet fragile Upon returning from exile, the Jews were more careful in observing the Lord's Law and recognized the High Priest as the religious head of the nation. However, their political situation remained vulnerable. Depending on circumstances and wars, they were subject to the power of Persia, Syria, or Egypt. ⚠️ Lesson: regaining freedom does not mean being free from all trials. A people may return to their land and still need vigilance, faithfulness, and prudence. The same is true in the home: overcoming a crisis is not enough; afterward comes the task of strengthening what is good and protecting the faith. 5 Antiochus Epiphanes and the test of faith Among the kings who ruled the region, some allowed the Jews to live in peace. Others tried to uproot them from their faith. One of the cruelest persecutors was Antiochus Epiphanes, king of Syria. He imposed a law that forced his subjects, under penalty of death, to accept the pagan religion. Some Jews yielded to the pressure, but many remained steadfast; others gave their lives rather than renounce the true faith. Among these martyrs are remembered the elderly Eleazar and the seven Maccabean brothers with their mother. 🔥 For families: there are goods higher than comfort, security, and even life itself. Sometimes faithfulness is tested not with words, but with concrete decisions. 6 The Maccabees: defense of faith and homeland In the face of Antiochus' persecution, brave defenders of the Jewish people's religion and independence arose. At the forefront was Mattathias, a faithful priest, along with his five sons. First, they withdrew to the mountains; there they gathered other determined men and began resistance against the oppressors. After Mattathias, his son Judas, called Maccabeus, continued the struggle. With God's help and the support of his brothers, he achieved important victories and established the Maccabean rule in Judea, which governed the people for about 128 years as both religious and military leaders, and later as kings. 7 Judas Maccabeus: courage, piety, and prayer for the dead Judas Maccabeus appears in Sacred Scripture as a man of great strength. He was not only a brave warrior: he also left an example of piety. After a battle, he ordered money to be collected and sent to Jerusalem so sacrifices could be offered for the fallen soldiers. This gesture confirms faith in prayer for the dead and purification after death, a teaching the Catholic tradition recognizes as linked to the doctrine of purgatory. Judas was blessed by his people and feared by his enemies. In the end, pressured by superior forces and lacking sufficient support from his own, he died fighting bravely in 161 BC. He was succeeded by his brothers Jonathan and Simon. Later, John Hyrcanus, Simon's son, ruled, remembered for his prudent and prosperous government. 8 When children lose their parents' virtue Over time, the descendants of those first Maccabees no longer retained the same virtue. Internal divisions, ambitions, and conflicts with powerful nations weakened Judea. The loss was not immediate, but progressive. The nation gradually lost strength and authority, until it fell under Roman rule. ⚠️ Warning for every family: the victories of one generation do not guarantee the faithfulness of the next. What parents conquer through sacrifice can be lost if children do not receive formation, example, and a sense of responsibility. 9 Rome, Herod, and the end of the kingdom of Judah The Romans first made Judea tributary. Then they imposed a foreign king: Herod, called the Great for some external works and successes. But his greatness was very limited from a moral standpoint. History remembers him for his intrigues, unjust actions, and ambition for power. Later, he would use that authority to persecute the Child Jesus. Herod had the appearance of success, but his life ended marked by misfortune: power without justice does not bring true greatness. After him, some of his sons and grandsons ruled, with varying authority. That glory lasted briefly. Finally, Judea was reduced to a province of the Roman Empire, under the rule of a governor sent by Rome. 10 The prophets: men sent to remember the truth Throughout Israel's history, God raised up prophets to uphold the people in the Law, correct them when they strayed, and protect them from idolatry. Idolatry was not merely a religious error: it was abandoning the true God to place trust in false gods, human powers, or pagan customs. For this reason, the prophets called the people to return to the Lord. Some prophets, such as Elijah and Elisha, left no written works, though their lives and actions are recorded in Sacred History. ✨ Major Prophets — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. They are called this because of the greater length of their books. 🕊️ Minor Prophets — The other twelve. Not because of lesser importance, but because of the brevity of their writings. 11 Their main mission: preparing the people for the Messiah The prophets did not only denounce sins or announce punishments. Their deepest mission was to keep alive the promise of the Messiah, the Savior promised by God. They prepared the people to recognize Him when He came. Centuries earlier, they announced aspects of His coming, His life, His passion, and His death. Viewed together, their words show a clear direction: the history of Israel was moving toward Christ. 12 Prophecies about the time of the Messiah's coming 📜 Daniel Announced that the Messiah would appear after a specified time of seventy weeks of years, that He would be rejected and killed, and that afterward Jerusalem would be destroyed and the people scattered. ⛪ Haggai and Malachi Indicated that the Messiah would come to the Second Temple. His coming therefore had to occur before the destruction of that Temple. ✨ Isaiah Besides announcing circumstances of the Messiah's birth and life, he indicated that after His coming the Gentiles would be called to faith. 🌍 Open salvation Salvation would not remain confined to one people but would extend to all nations. 13 Fulfillment in Jesus Christ History confirmed those signs: the foretold time was fulfilled, Jerusalem was destroyed, the Second Temple vanished, the Jewish people were scattered, and many Gentiles embraced the faith. Therefore, according to Christian faith, the promised Messiah has already come. All these prophecies find their full fulfillment in one person: our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the true Messiah awaited by Israel and announced by the prophets. ✝️ What this story teaches families This stage of Sacred History leaves several lessons for the home: 🔥 Daniel Faithfulness can be maintained even in a foreign land. 🌿 The return Rebuilding requires patience, as when returning from exile. 👑 Esther Providence can act through a courageous person. 🛡️ The Maccabees Faith is defended when it is sought to be torn from the heart of the people. 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Transmission What is not formed in children can be lost in a single generation. ⭐ The meaning History does not advance aimlessly: God prepared His people for centuries to receive the Savior. “Seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness.” — Mt 6:33 Recommended Products St. Joseph Edition, Catholic Bible View on Amazon Catechism of Saint Pius X View on Amazon 1962 Roman Daily Missal View on Amazon Revelations View on Amazon Hell and Its Torments View on Amazon The place where God dwells View on Amazon As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. articles.title: New Testament Summary (1): From the Annunciation to the Raising of Lazarus
articles.text: The Public Life of Jesus (Part 1): From the Annunciation to Lazarus 📖 New Testament · Part 1 From the Annunciation to the resurrection of Lazarus Told to be read as a family. Inspired by A Short History of Religion in The Catechism of Saint Pius X. In this journey God prepares the Savior Visit to Elizabeth Birth in Bethlehem Presentation in the Temple Adoration of the Magi Flight to Egypt Jesus at twelve years old John the Baptist Baptism and temptations First disciples Miracle at Cana The twelve Apostles Preaching of the Kingdom The miracles Opposition grows 1 God prepares the coming of the Savior During the reign of Herod the Great, Mary and Joseph lived in Nazareth. Both descended from King David, but led a simple life sustained by their own work. Joseph was recognized as a just man, and Mary had consecrated her entire life to God. Then God sent the archangel Gabriel to announce to Mary that she had been chosen as Mother of the Savior. The angel greeted her as “full of grace” and explained that she would conceive by the work of the Holy Spirit, without losing her virginity. «Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word.» Mary’s response · Lk 1:38 At that instant the Incarnation occurred: the eternal Son of God assumed human nature without ceasing to be God. Thus began the work of redemption of all humanity. 2 The visit to Elizabeth and the birth of John the Baptist After the Annunciation, Mary traveled to the hill country of Judea to visit her cousin Elizabeth, who was expecting a child despite her advanced age. More than a family visit, it was to help and serve her for several months. When Elizabeth heard her greeting, she recognized by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit that Mary carried the Messiah in her womb, and called her Mother of her Lord. Mary responded with the hymn of the Magnificat , a song of praise and gratitude that the Church continues to pray to this day. Elizabeth’s son was John the Baptist, chosen by God to prepare the people for the coming of Jesus Christ. 3 The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem A decree from Emperor Caesar Augustus ordered a census throughout the Roman Empire. Because they belonged to the family of David, Joseph and Mary had to travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem. Upon arrival, they found the city full of travelers and could not find lodging. They took shelter in a place intended for animals and there, during the night, Jesus was born. Mary wrapped the Child in swaddling clothes and laid Him in a manger. That same night, an angel announced the good news to some shepherds who were watching their flocks: they were the first to visit and adore the Savior. 4 The presentation of Jesus in the Temple Eight days after His birth, the Child received the name of Jesus, as the angel had indicated. When the days prescribed by the Law were fulfilled, Mary and Joseph took Him to the Temple of Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord. There the old man Simeon recognized Jesus as the promised Messiah and gave thanks to God with the canticle of the Nunc dimittis . The prophetess Anna also praised God and spoke of the Child to those who awaited the deliverance of Israel. 5 The adoration of the Magi Some time later, wise men from the East arrived, guided by an extraordinary star. They understood that it announced the birth of the awaited King and traveled to pay Him homage. First they passed through Jerusalem, where Herod pretended interest in knowing the Child. Then they continued to Bethlehem, where they found Jesus with Mary. Prostrate before Him, they offered Him three gifts laden with meaning: 🥇 Gold — recognition of His kingship. 🕊️ Incense — homage to His divinity. 🌿 Myrrh — remembrance of His future passion and death. Warned by God in dreams, they returned to their country without informing Herod. 6 The flight to Egypt Seeing that the Magi would not return, Herod ordered the killing of all the young children in Bethlehem, intending to eliminate Jesus as well. Before this happened, an angel warned Joseph in a dream to flee with Mary and the Child to Egypt. The Holy Family remained there until the death of Herod and then returned, settling permanently in Nazareth. 7 Jesus in the Temple at twelve years old Every year Mary and Joseph made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to celebrate Passover. When Jesus was twelve years old, He remained in the Temple without their noticing. After searching for Him anxiously for three days, they found Him conversing with the teachers of the Law, who admired His wisdom. When Mary asked Him why He had stayed there, Jesus replied: «Did you not know that I must be about my Father’s business?» Words of Jesus · Lk 2:49 With these words He manifested His unique relationship with God the Father. Then He returned to Nazareth and continued to live obediently with Mary and Joseph, growing in wisdom, stature, and grace. 8 John the Baptist prepares the way When the time appointed by God arrived, John the Baptist began to preach beside the Jordan River. He dressed simply, led a life of penance, and invited everyone to convert: «Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.» Preaching of John · Mt 3:2 Many people came to listen to him and receive baptism as a sign of conversion. 9 The baptism and temptations of Jesus When Jesus was about thirty years old, He went to the Jordan to be baptized by John. Although John considered himself unworthy to do so, he obeyed the will of the Lord. As Jesus came out of the water, the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in the form of a dove and the voice of the Father was heard: «This is my beloved Son.» Voice of the Father · Mt 3:17 Afterward, Jesus withdrew to the desert for forty days to pray and fast. There He allowed Himself to be tempted by the devil and overcame every temptation, teaching us how to remain faithful to God in the face of evil. 10 The first disciples Upon His return, John the Baptist pointed to Jesus saying: «Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.» Testimony of John · Jn 1:29 Some disciples then began to follow Jesus. Among them were Andrew and Simon, to whom Jesus gave the name of Peter. Little by little other men also responded to His call, beginning the group that would accompany the Lord throughout His mission. 11 The first miracle at Cana Jesus attended a wedding in Cana of Galilee with His Mother and some disciples. When the wine ran out, Mary discreetly presented the need to her Son. Jesus turned a large quantity of water into excellent wine. This was the Lord’s first public miracle and strengthened the faith of those who were beginning to follow Him. 12 The choice of the twelve Apostles Later, Jesus chose twelve men to live with Him and continue His mission: Peter Andrew James John Philip Bartholomew Matthew Thomas James (of Alphaeus) Judas Thaddaeus Simon the Canaanite Judas Iscariot Among them, Jesus entrusted Peter with a special responsibility as the visible head of the apostolic group. 13 The preaching of the Kingdom of God For about three years, Jesus traveled through Judea and Galilee announcing the coming of the Kingdom of God. He taught in synagogues and in the open air —on mountains, in villages, in houses, and by the sea— addressing people of every condition. Among His best-known teachings are the Sermon on the Mount and the prayer of the Our Father , with which He taught His disciples to address the heavenly Father. He frequently used parables to explain the truths of the Kingdom through simple examples from daily life. Among the best known are: The prodigal son The good Samaritan The good shepherd The sower The mustard seed The ten virgins 14 The miracles that confirmed His mission Jesus’ words were accompanied by numerous works of mercy. He healed the sick, restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the mute; He cleansed lepers and freed many people from the dominion of evil spirits. On two occasions He fed large crowds by multiplying a few loaves and fishes. And He performed several miracles over death, such as the resurrection of the son of the widow of Nain and, shortly before His Passion, that of Lazarus, who had been in the tomb for four days. ✨ A testimony of the Father: all these signs confirmed that Jesus was the promised Messiah and the true Son of God. In the Transfiguration, the Father again proclaimed Him His beloved Son. 15 The growing opposition against Jesus While many people welcomed His teaching with faith, the principal religious leaders began to reject Him. His denunciation of hypocrisy, together with the popularity of His preaching and His miracles, aroused the envy of scribes, Pharisees, and other leaders of the people, who sought to discredit Him and find grounds to accuse Him. The resurrection of Lazarus caused even more people to believe in Jesus, which increased the fear of His adversaries. Finally they decided to seek a way to put Him to death. Without understanding the scope of his words, the high priest Caiaphas stated that it was better for one man to die for the people. That phrase unknowingly announced the redemptive sacrifice that Jesus Christ would offer for the salvation of the world. 🕊️ Everything was being prepared From Mary’s “be it done” to the shadow of the cross that was already approaching, each step led to one and the same end: the redemption of the world. Here ends the first part. What Caiaphas said without understanding would soon be fulfilled, and death would not have the last word. articles.title: True Revealed: Understanding Truth Through the Bible
articles.text: The Revealed Truth: Bible in Family Life  The Word as the Heart of the Home The Christian home –ecclesia domestica– is called to be a sanctuary where the Word of God resounds with the same authority with which it is proclaimed in the liturgy. 1  Biblical Foundation Divine mandate Dt 6,6-9; Jos 24,15 God asks that His Law be "repeated to the children" and inscribed in the customs of the home. Redemptive memory Ps 78,5-7 Recounting the works of God ensures that the next generation does not forget His wonders. Life in Christ 2 Tim 3,14-17 Scripture instructs, corrects, and prepares "the man of God for every good work". Domestic ecclesiality Col 3,16; Eph 5,19 "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly." Singing and shared reading build charity. Saint John Chrysostom: "Make your home a church; there peace reigns and the devil flees" (Hom. in Eph 20) 2  Spiritual Benefits 1 Sacramental unity The Word heard and discussed in the family acts as a pre-spiritual communion, orienting hearts toward Sunday Eucharist. 2 Moral discernment By confronting culture with Revelation, members gain sound judgment against ideologies contrary to human dignity. 3 Transmission of faith The practical experience of reading, praying, and discussing Scripture engrains the depositum fidei in the affective memory of children. 4 Strength in trials Families who daily savor biblical consolation show greater resilience in the face of economic, cultural, or spiritual crises. 5 Fostering prayer Reading naturally leads to praise, thanksgiving, and intercession, perfecting family prayer. 3  How to Begin 1 Choosing the sacred text Acquire a Catholic Bible with 73 books, preferably with brief introductions and notes. 2 Write a "yes, Lord" into the calendar Set aside a fixed daily moment (10-15 min) and mark it as non-negotiable, like a medical appointment. 3 Create a symbolic place Place the Bible enthroned on a simple stand, with a candle or icon that recalls the presence of Christ-the-Word. 4 Roles and participation Assign roles: main reader, antiphon reader (children), and reflection guide (father or mother). 5 Lectio-dialogical method Lectio (attentive reading)  Brief silence  Resonance (each shares a phrase that touched them)  Oratio (spontaneous petitions)  Conclusion with the Our Father. 4  Practical Suggestions  Frequency and duration Beginners: 3 days a week, 10 min. Intermediate: Monday to Friday, 15 min. Advanced: daily lectio with responsorial psalm; on Sundays, commentary on the Sunday Gospel.  Contextualization For families with young children, it is helpful to begin with an illustrated Bible or short dramatizations.  Rotation of genres 1 week narratives (Genesis), 1 week psalms, 1 week Gospel, 1 week epistles; avoid monotony.  Memory dynamics During the week, each child memorizes a verse and applies it in a concrete act of fraternal charity.  Sunday synthesis At the end of the week, each member shares the passage that transformed them the most and why.  Atmosphere Reduce distractions: devices off the table, warm lighting, 2 minutes of prior silence. 5  Recommended Biblical Passages Level Theme Suggested text Reason Initiation ( 10 years) Creation Gen 1,1-2,3 Clear narrative, wonder at divine work. Good Shepherd Ps 23 Familiar image, filial trust. Multiplication of loaves Jn 6,1-15 Teaches providence and solidarity. Growth (11-15 years) Youth vocation 1 Sam 3,1-10 Identity and listening. Parable of the prodigal son Lk 15,11-32 Mercy and responsible freedom. Armor of God Eph 6,10-18 Spiritual struggle, appealing symbolism. Maturity ( 16 years) Practical wisdom Jas 1,19-27 Faith-works coherence. Conjugal charity Eph 5,21-33 Theology of marriage. Eschatological hope Rev 21,1-7 Eternal horizon, steadfastness in trials.  Why a Catholic Bible with 73 books The Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, defined in the councils of Hippo (393), Carthage III (397), and solemnly ratified at the Council of Trent (1546) the canon that includes the so-called deuterocanonical books. These texts –Wisdom, Sirach, 1-2 Maccabees, Tobit, Judith, and Baruch– enrich family catechesis with crucial themes: martyrdom for the faith, the intercession of the saints, purifying almsgiving, divine providence in domestic life. Using an incomplete Bible would impoverish the experience and fracture doctrinal unity with the universal Church.   Conclusion Incorporating Sacred Scripture into family life is not a pious addition, but an act of loving obedience that sustains parental authority, strengthens the virtue of children, and makes the home a beacon that radiates the light of Christ in the midst of a frequently adverse culture.  Question for family dialogue: After the first week of reading, which word or verse would you like to see more fully embodied in our family, and how could we cooperate with grace to achieve it? 📖 Recommended Bibles The Catholic Youth Bible View on Amazon The Didache Bible: Ignatius Bible View on Amazon New American Bible, Revised Edition View on Amazon As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases. articles.title: Christian Petitions: How to Pray with Faith and Purpose
articles.text: Church Petitions Explained: Simple Christian Guide ⛪ Christian Petitions Inspired by the Solemn Prayers of Good Friday This guide explains, in simple words, 9 ideas and people for whom the Catholic Church traditionally prays very solemnly on Good Friday. 📝 Note: we quote the core of each petition in Latin (not the entire text) and provide its meaning in English. Full formulas can be found in the indicated sources. ⛪ 1) The Holy Church In the square, a very diverse group of people shares food at a fundraiser: everyone speaks differently, but all help. The Church is the great family of Jesus’ followers spread throughout the world; its mission is to lead us to God through faith, prayer, and good works. Petition (Latin): "Oremus, dilectissimi nobis, pro Ecclesia sancta Dei: ut eam… pacificare, adunare et custodire dignetur…" Meaning in English: "Let us pray for the holy Church, that God may grant it peace, unity, and protection throughout the earth." ✨ Remember: The Church is a universal family called to serve and love. 👨‍🦳 2) The Supreme Pontiff (the Pope) On the news, you see the Pope visiting the sick. You wonder: "Who keeps so many Christians united?" The Pope, successor of St. Peter, encourages the faith and safeguards the unity of the Church. Petition (Latin): "Oremus et pro beatissimo Papa nostro N., ut Deus… salvum atque incolumem custodiat Ecclesiae suae sanctae…" Meaning in English: "Let us pray for the Pope, that God may preserve and support him in the service of His Church." ✨ Remember: We pray for the one who visibly guides Christians. 🙏 3) Bishops, priests, deacons… and all God’s People At the parish, some sing, others read, others distribute food; the priest leads the prayer. Each one contributes something. The Church has ordained ministers (bishops, priests, and deacons) and faithful with various services. All are necessary. Petition (Latin): "Oremus et pro omnibus Episcopis, Presbyteris, Diaconibus… et pro omni populo sancto Dei." Meaning in English: "Let us pray for all ministers and for all the holy people of God, that we may serve faithfully." ✨ Remember: In the Church there is a diversity of tasks and one mission: to love and serve. 💧 4) Catechumens (those preparing for Baptism) A friend tells you she wants to be baptized and starts learning to pray: she is excited and nervous. Catechumens are those who ask for Baptism and prepare to follow Christ. Petition (Latin): "Oremus et pro catechumenis nostris: ut Deus… adaperiat aures praecordiorum ipsorum…" Meaning in English: "Let us pray for the catechumens, that God may open their hearts and lead them with joy to Baptism." ✨ Remember: Faith begins with a “yes” that God Himself helps us to give. 🤲 5) People in need You think of a sick neighbor and a cousin traveling: heartfelt words of intercession come to you. We pray for those who suffer: illness, poverty, prison, dangerous journeys, or sadness. Petition (Latin): "Oremus… ut mundum purget erroribus: morbos auferat: famem depellat… infirmantibus sanitatem…" Meaning in English: "Let us ask God to remove the errors and evils of the world: to heal, deliver, provide work, health, safe return, and help to all." ✨ Remember: God is moved by our sorrows and hears our pleas. 🔄 6) Those separated from the Catholic faith (heretics and schismatics) On the Internet, you read debates among Christians who no longer share the same teaching or have left common communion. The Church prays for the baptized who have departed from the truth of faith or visible unity, that they may return. Petition (Latin): "Oremus et pro haereticis et schismaticis: ut Deus… eruat eos ab erroribus… et ad sanctam matrem Ecclesiam revocare dignetur." Meaning in English: "Let us pray for them, that God may free them from error and bring them back to the unity of the Church." ✨ Remember: Charity seeks truth and unity, without insults or contempt. ✡️ 7) The Jews (religious sense, not ethnic) Studying the Bible, you discover that Jesus was born of the Jewish people and that the first disciples quoted the prophets. The Church prays respectfully for the Jewish people that God may enlighten them to recognize Jesus Christ. (Today, when celebrating with the 1962 Missal, the formula revised by Benedict XVI in 2008 is used). Petition (Latin): "Oremus et pro Iudaeis: ut Deus… illuminet corda eorum, ut agnoscant Iesum Christum salvatorem omnium hominum." Meaning in English: "Let us pray for the Jews, that God may enlighten their hearts to recognize Jesus, the Savior of all." ✨ Remember: We ask for the salvation of all peoples. 🤔 8) Those who do not believe in God (pagans or non-believers) You think of a classmate who believes in nothing; you decide to treat him with friendship and pray for him. The Church prays for those who do not know God, that they may abandon what keeps them away and discover the living and true God. Petition (Latin): "Oremus et pro paganis: ut Deus omnipotens auferat iniquitatem a cordibus eorum… convertantur ad Deum vivum et verum…" Meaning in English: "Let us pray for non-believers, that God may change their hearts and draw them closer to Him." ✨ Remember: God desires life and joy for all. 🏛️ 9) Rulers and civil authorities You hear a law on education and family being debated; you realize that, in addition to giving your opinion, it is good to pray. We pray for rulers, that God may guide their minds and hearts toward the common good and peace. Petition (Latin): "Oremus et pro omnibus res publicas moderantibus… ut Deus… mentes et corda eorum… dirigat ad nostram perpetuam pacem." Meaning in English: "Let us pray for those in authority, that they may promote peace, the good of families, and respect for faith." ✨ Remember: Prayer for authorities seeks true peace and justice. 🏠 To pray at home (very simple) 1 Choose one of these intentions each day. 2 Say together: "Lord Jesus, we ask You for… (mention the intention)". 3 Keep one minute of silence. 4 Finish with an Our Father. 📚 Sources of the Latin text (Traditional Missal / Good Friday prayers): collections of the traditional liturgy with the Latin text of the Orationes sollemnes (including the 2008 formula for the petition for the Jews).
